description.summary: applications export their menus; the shell renders them

protocol.description:
On Trinix the menu bar belongs to the screen, not to the window. An application therefore does not draw its menus — it describes them, and the shell draws the menus of whichever application is active, at the top of the display, in one consistent style.
A menu belongs to an *application*, and the application here is the connection: a client asks for one menu bar and it covers every window that client opens. That is what the system being imitated does — the bar is a property of the application object, so moving between two windows of one application changes nothing the user can see — and it is the only scoping under which an application whose windows are all closed still has a menu bar, which is how the user opens a new window from an application that has none. A window whose menus genuinely differ says so with `get_toplevel_menu_bar`, and that is expected to be rare.
Which window has focus does still reach the menu, but only through item *state*: an application greys an item out with `update` when the focused window cannot do it. It decides whether Save is available; it does not decide whether the File menu exists.
Why a Wayland protocol rather than D-Bus, which is what every previous global-menu implementation used:
A menu has to ride something whose lifetime and focus the compositor already tracks, and D-Bus has no notion of either. The established designs work around that by exporting the menu on the bus and then using a Wayland (or X11) protocol anyway, purely to say which client the bus name belongs to — so the D-Bus route costs two IPC mechanisms, two lifetimes to reconcile, and menus that outlive their owner by however long the bus takes to notice. Carrying the model on the Wayland connection makes the association structural: the menu is created from the connection, dies with it, and arrives in order with the rest of that client's state. The mistake those designs made was the bus, not the choice of object to hang a menu on.
What that costs is having to define a menu model here, which the rest of this file is. It is a flat set of nodes addressed by client-assigned id and linked by parent — a tree, expressed the way a tree survives being mutated incrementally.
Interoperating with toolkits that already speak D-Bus menus is a bridge over this protocol, and deliberately not a second path through it.
Warning! This protocol is Trinix's own and is not stable.

interface.name: trinix_menu_manager_v1

description.summary: hands out menus, for a client or for one of its windows

interface.description:
Two scopes, and the first is the ordinary one. `get_menu_bar` is the application's, `get_toplevel_menu_bar` is an override for a single window; the shell shows the focused window's override if it has one, that window's client's bar otherwise, and its own if nothing is focused.
This interface is still version 1 although it once took a toplevel and now does not. That is deliberate: the audience for a version bump is whoever would have to keep both shapes working, nothing had shipped against the first one, and a version 2 that exists to be polite to nobody is a version 2 that has to be carried forever. The protocol says at the top that it is not stable, and this is what that sentence is for.

request.name: destroy
request.description: Menus created from it are unaffected.

request.name: get_menu_bar
request.description:
The bar is shown whenever any of this client's windows is active, and it is not attached to any one of them: moving between two windows of the same application leaves the bar exactly as it was, which is the behaviour being imitated and is why this request names no toplevel.
It also outlives all of them. An application with every window closed still has a menu bar, and that is not a curiosity — it is how the user gets a window back.
It is a protocol error for a client to ask for a second one.

request.name: get_toplevel_menu_bar

description.summary: override the menu bar for one window

request.description:
For the window whose menus genuinely are not the application's — an inspector, a console, a document of a different kind. While this toplevel is active the shell shows this menu in place of the client's bar; the client's bar is untouched and returns when focus moves on.
A separate request rather than an optional argument on `get_menu_bar`, so that an application which never wants an override never mentions a toplevel, and so that "has a menu bar already" stays a question with one answer per scope rather than one answer for both.
The override is withdrawn when the toplevel goes away. It is a protocol error to ask for a second one for the same toplevel.

entry.name: already_has_menu
entry.summary: the client, or the toplevel, already exported a menu bar

entry.name: bad_item
entry.summary: an item id was zero, duplicated, or unknown

entry.name: bad_parent
entry.summary: the parent id is not a submenu

interface.name: trinix_menu_v1
interface.description:
Whether this is a client's bar or one window's override was settled by the request that created it and never changes afterwards. Nothing else in this interface differs between the two, which is the point of splitting them at the manager: the scope is a fact about the object, not a mode the client has to keep in mind on every call.
Changes are accumulated and applied atomically by `commit`, for the same reason surface state is: a menu that is half-rebuilt must never be a menu the user can see, let alone click.
Item ids are chosen by the client, must be non-zero, and must be unique within this menu. Id 0 is the menu bar itself, and is the parent of the top-level menus.
A client is free to describe the whole menu up front, or to describe only the bar and fill each menu in when `about_to_show` arrives. The second is what an application with a large or expensive menu should do, and the protocol is shaped so that it costs nothing extra.

request.name: insert
request.description: `index` is the position among `parent`'s existing children; a negative index appends. Inserting an item whose id already exists is a protocol error — use `update`.

arg.name: id
arg.summary: client-assigned, non-zero, unique in this menu

arg.name: label
arg.summary: with an underscore before the mnemonic, if any

request.name: update
request.description: Keeps the item's identity, its position and its children, which is what makes it safe to call on every state change without the open menu flickering.

request.name: set_accelerator

description.summary: give an item a keyboard shortcut

request.description:
The shell both displays this and honours it: a shortcut on a menu item works whether or not the menu has ever been opened, which is the behaviour users expect and the reason the shell needs to know about it rather than the application handling the key itself.
A keysym of zero removes the accelerator.

description.summary: delete an item and its children

request.name: commit

description.summary: apply everything since the last commit

request.description: A commit with no pending changes is valid and does nothing.

event.name: activated
event.description: Sent for leaf items only. For a checkbox or a radio item the client is responsible for deciding the new state and sending `update`: the shell does not assume a click toggles anything, because whether it does is the application's business.

event.name: about_to_show

description.summary: a submenu is about to open

event.description: The client may mutate the menu and commit; the shell shows the menu on the next commit, or immediately if none arrives promptly. An application that populates lazily should do it here.

event.name: closed
event.description: Nothing is open any more, whether because the user chose something or because they dismissed it.

entry.name: checkbox
entry.summary: an item with an independent on/off state

entry.name: radio
entry.summary: one of a set; siblings of the same kind are exclusive

entry.name: checked
entry.summary: ticked, for a checkbox or radio item

entry.name: hidden
entry.summary: present in the model but not shown
